en: Now, for the sake of turning back the state of being a bound soul within the continuum of one's own bondage, and for the manifestation of Śiva-nature, the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) is proclaimed here. || 1 ||
The path of reality, the path of words, the path of phonemes consisting of worlds, the path of mantras, and the path of kalās—all these enter into the single state of Śiva. ||2||
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease;
subtle, all-pervading, eternal, constant, imperishable, and sovereign. || 3 ||
It is immeasurable because it is infinite; it is indescribable because it lacks defining characteristics;
it is incomparable because it has no likeness; and it is free from affliction because it is stainless.
It is subtle because it is unperceivable; it is all-pervading because of its omnipresence;
it is eternal because it is devoid of a cause; and it is stable because of its immobility. || 5 ||
Because it is imperishable due to its perfection, and because it is the state of the Lord,
this Śiva-tattva is declared to be situated above all paths.
Through its nature as the syllable Oṃ, the supreme Śiva shines forth, transcending tranquility;
seated in the center of the seed-lotus, the Lord is the face of the entire path.
Then, the principle of Sadāśiva, situated in the four quarters,
was pervaded by the seed-syllable as before, which abides in the state of universal withdrawal.
Śiva, whose body consists of the five mantras, abides in the station of the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
The path of peace is the path known as Mantra, consisting of nine manifestations beginning with the syllables.
Extending from the form of space (vyoman) down to the earth (rūpa), it is situated within the seven-syllable word;
it is the two infinite powers: the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and the power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 10 ||
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—this is the triad of powers (śaktitraya) beyond this;
it is established in two states, beginning with the All (Sarva) and ending with Śiva. || 11 ||
Below that is the principle of Īśvara, situated within the group of eight beginning with Ananta;
at the conclusion of meditation, it is encircled by seed-syllables and established at the end of the womb.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, the third Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and thereafter Trimūrti. || 13 ||
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin, the lords of the lords of Vidyās and Avidyās—these eight are established respectively in the eight stages at the end of the Śānti level. 14.

One should know the *vidyātattva* as being situated within the lotus-like series of words beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *śiva*, and as established at the beginning of the path of knowledge (*vidyādhvan*). || 15 ||
The body of the Queen of the Embodiment of Knowledge is not overcome by the sequence of the Rudra-array;
it is encircled by the path of the seed-syllables situated within the womb-place. 16.
The array of knowledge (vidyā-vyūha) is to be known as residing in the syllable; it begins with Vāmadeva and is supreme.
It remains for nine kalpas and serves as the support for the path to liberation. || 17 ||
The array known as Vigraheśvara, consisting of eight [deities] beginning with Aghora,
is established in embodied form within the supreme state known as Anantīna.
Ambakā, Brahmavetālī, Bhṛguṇī, Sthāṇumatī, Rūpiṇī, Mahājvālā, and the renowned Mālinī are the supreme [goddesses]. || 19 ||
Suveṭālī, Gaurī, Nandinī, and Aghorā—these stood in the array of the King of Vidyās in the supreme state. || 20 ||
Then, in the fourth [section], there is the array of the limbs consisting of the five Vidyāṅgas, the Rudras, the Krodhas, the Asthiśṛṅkhalās, and those born from the withdrawal of the weapons.
Halāhala, Samātaṅga, the one known as Nīlalohita, Icchumbha, Śabara, Caṇḍa, Vaṭarudra, and Mahābala—[these are the eight]. 22.
These Rudras, surrounded by many powerful Rudras,
abide here in the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva) as a fivefold array, occupying the fifth station.
The station of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), ending with Īśāna, is situated there;
below that is the Māyā-tattva, surrounded by sixteen seed-syllables within a hexagon.
There, eight lords of the mandalas are situated in order starting from the east;
at their tip stands the supreme Bhuvaneśa, the size of a thumb.
Īśāna, Ekapiṅga, and then Udbhava;
Bhava, Vāmadeva, and thereafter Mahātejas. || 26 ||
Below Māyā, the principle of Time (kālatattva) is situated within those two feet;
Niyati is in the other [foot], and then Kalā and Vidya follow.
These four principles are each individually enveloped by the arrangement of seed-syllables situated within the letters beginning with 'śa' and ending with 'ra', as previously described.
Here, the Rudras, beginning with Śikheda and ending with Krodheśa, each individually occupy the row extending from the secret place (guhya) up to the void (vyoman). || 29 ||
Śikheda, Ekavīra, Pañcāntaka, Sūraga, Jyotiḥpiṅga, Saṃvarta, Caṇḍa, and again Krodheśvara; || 30 ||
Below those, situated thirty-two steps from the Pratiṣṭhā level, is the remaining path of Nivṛtti; thus is the Path of Kalā proclaimed. || 31 ||
The principle of passion (rāgatattva) is situated within the fivefold foundation and so forth;
it is encompassed by the sixteen-fold [principle] established in the station of the womb.
In this same way, the remaining principles (tattvas) are each individually enveloped by the array of seed-syllables (bījavyūha) situated within the letters from 'A' to 'KṢ', as previously described.
Below that principle of Rāga, those who know the principles recognize the principle of Puruṣa, which is endowed with three principles and situated in six stages.
Among those two groups, there are ten Rudras situated in the series of words beginning with Vyāna and ending with Ānanda; and Śiva stands as the eleventh among those Rudras at the very beginning.
Ananta, Aja, Umākānta, Pracaṇḍa, Ekavīraka, Sarveśāna, Īśvara, Bhava, Ugra, Bhīma, and Vāmaka. || 36 ||
Established one by one in succession upon this stainless path,
they bestow desired enjoyments for the sake of the satisfaction of the enjoyer.
Then follows the principle of Pradhāna, which resides in the group of eight beginning with incense;
there, moreover, are the eight stations of the Yogins situated in those very places. || 38 ||
The Śraikaṇṭha, Mauma, Kaumāra, Vaiṣṇava, and Brāhma, as well as the Raibhava, Kṛta, and likewise the Akṛta. || 39 ||
The eightfold divine womb (devayoni) is established within those eight words beginning with Nidhana;
therein, starting from the beginning, it culminates in the state of Brahman.
The Prājāpatya, the Soma, the Āindra, the Gāndharva, the Yākṣa, and thereafter the Rākṣasa, and finally the eighth, the Paiśāca. || 41 ||
From Pradhāna arises the principle of Buddhi, situated in the station called Nidhana;
likewise, Ahaṅkāra is in another, and Manas in two stations beyond that. 42.

The sense organs belong to these two alone; here, in Śiva, are the organs of cognition, and in the principle called Ahaṃkāra (the Ego), the organs of action. Thus are the principles in these two stages.
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose;
likewise the organ of speech, the hands, the generative organ, and finally the anus and the feet. 44.
The five elements, preceded by the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), are established respectively in these five stages, beginning with the Supreme Self (paramātman). 45.
From that [source] arise the elements beginning with space; then follow four stages, and from the stage of great splendor (mahātejas) again, four more are established.
Among them, five groups of eight are situated; in those five, there are five arrays.
These begin with Sthāṇvaṣṭaka; listen now as they are described.
Chagalaṇḍa, Duraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kāla, Cara, as well as Śaṅkukarṇa and Sthaleśvara are located there. 48.
Then there is the celebrated site of Sthūleśvara, followed by Sthāṇvaṣṭaka,
Vastrapāda, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya.
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Suvarṇa, Sthāṇu, and Aṣṭaka—this group of eight is known as the Pavitrāṣṭaka; this sacred site is to be resorted to for the service of the field (kṣetra).
Gaya and Kurukṣetra, Nakhala and Kakshala, as well as Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Māhendra, and Bhīmakeśvara. || 51 ||
This third [set] is secret; now the fourth is being declared: Hariścandra, Suśaila, Jalpa, and Āmrātikeśvara. 52.
Madhyama, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava—this is the secret beyond secrets, which is now called "pertaining to each individual self. (53)
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara;
Āṣāḍhīśa, Caṇḍīśa, Bhārabhūti, and Lākula.
This fifth element is indeed proclaimed as having the nature of water;
below those, O Brahmin, is the earthly principle, known from the Veda as "Om."
And the western [section] is situated within the words beginning with *bhava* and ending with the first letter;
it is encircled, as before, by an array of seed-syllables (*bīja*) residing in the intermediate letters. 56.
He is the Lord of all the lords of the worlds, from Brahmā to Īśāna;
his body resembles shimmering rays, and the crescent moon rests upon his head.

He was surrounded on the ten directions by the hundred Rudras stationed at their respective places— Śambhu, the all-pervading lord of the Gaṇas, the three-eyed one, who is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Saṃvāha, Vivāja, and the far-sighted Nabholipsu, endowed with sovereign power, having assailed the army of Śambhu, [advanced]. || 59 ||
The great gods wander about, well-honored by the lords of those directions:
Ananta, Pālaka, the heroic Vṛṣa, and the lord of Pātāla.
The bull, the devourer, the bright, the red, and the one facing all directions—
having overcome these, they are endowed with infinite strength and sovereign power.
The great gods, highly honored by Vāyurāja, roam about;
the lord of the Vidyādharas, who is all-knowing and has mastered the Vedas, protects them. 62.
He who is clothed in bark, the tawny-eyed, the guardian of beings, the lover of offerings,
the lord of all sciences, the sustainer, and likewise the creator of pleasure and pain.
These ten powerful Rudras are stationed in the northeast;
having assumed the strength of Īśāna, they are endowed with sovereign power.
The great gods, well-honored by the lords of the quarters, roam about;
likewise, he who wears a crown of matted locks and bears various jewels [is there]. 65.
The lord of treasures, handsome, fortunate, and one who crushes with his gentle body;
he is of a most gracious luster, able to assume any form at will, and very dear.
Someśās are fully described as being established in the station of Sāṃnaidhya;
having seized the power of Soma, they are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods, highly honored by Soma, roam about;
they are swift, light, possessing the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, and the bringers of destruction at the end of time.
Wearing five tufts of hair, with matted locks, and possessing a voice like the roar of clouds,
they have assumed the strength of the wind and are endowed with sovereign power.
The great gods, highly honored by Vāyu-rāja, roam about—
Bala, Atibala, and the mighty Pāśahasta.
And then Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, Balāntaka,
Vaḍavāmukha, and Bhīma were stationed in the western quarter.
Bestowing desired enjoyments upon gods, dānavas, and mortals,
they have overcome the power of Varuṇa, endowed as they are with sovereign might.
The great gods, well-honored by Varuṇa and Īśa, roam about;
there is Nairṛta, the slayer and destroyer, terrifying with his cruel gaze. (73)
With upward-pointing phalli, deformed eyes, smoke-colored complexions, and blood-red glances,
they were endowed with sovereign power as they overcame the strength of Nirṛti.
The great gods, highly honored by the king of the Rākṣasas, roam about:
Yāmya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and the one known as Karta.
Time is known as the husband of Dharma; it is the uniter and the cause of separation.
Having overcome the power of Yama, they are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods, highly honored by Dharmarāja, wander about:
Agni, Rudra, Hlātāśī, Piṅgaṇḍa, Svādaka, and Hara. (77)
Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmānta, Ugha, Kṣayāntaka—having seized the power of Agni, they were endowed with the energy of Vahni. 78.
The great gods, highly honored by Tejorāja, roam about:
Kapālīśa, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha, and Pramardana. (79)
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa—endowed with sovereign power, they overcame the strength of Indra. 80.
The great gods, highly honored by Śakra, the king of gods, roam about;
the hosts of the hundred Rudras are established in the exterior egg. 81.
Now, the path (adhvan) of that which resides within is described as it truly exists:
Satya, Tapa, Jana, from that Maha, and then Svar and Bhuvaḥ. || 82 ||
The world of Bhūr and these seven others are situated respectively in these stations;
there dwell Brahmā, the sons of Brahmā, and the lords, who have turned away from worldly existence and travel in celestial chariots.
And the homeless humans are established in seven groups across the seven [worlds],
while the seven netherworlds (pātālas) are likewise situated within the seven steps.
Bala is known as Vitala, and then Nitala, Sutala, Talātala, and another known as Rasātala. (85)
And the seventh, well-known as Mahātala, O one of sharp intellect, is there where nine thousand nāgas always dwell by the thousands. || 86 ||
Those heroes, who always enjoy pleasures and possess strength of incomparable vigor, remain established in the state of "Śivāya" after [passing through] Naraka and Raurava. 87.
Kumbhīpāka and Avīci are situated in the pair of natis respectively;
from those, Rudra as Kālānala is established at the end in the syllable *sa*.
Rest (*virāma*) is said by Anaya, which has no beginning here in this world. 88.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Paths (*adhvan*), in the *Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha*.
